title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction

paper.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
paper.abstract:
Abstract Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and
each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks
which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of
the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with
per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy
collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades
at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only
once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers.
Modeling eviction as a top- k k cut, we compute answer survival probability
from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach
selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and
the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never
significantly below it.
It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with
significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the
default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer
while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18
to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries
over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with
no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where
several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default.
On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader
at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering
(LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The KV cache is the memory cost of long-context inference, and eviction is the simplest way to shrink it: score every cached token, keep the top k k , drop the rest. Existing methods differ in how they score and how they spend the budget ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Cai et al., 2024 ) , but all take scores from the layer whose cache is pruned: layer 7 judges what layer 7 keeps. The scoring layer is a hyperparameter that, to our knowledge, no eviction method varies or reports. We find that the chosen layer’s depth governs eviction quality at every scale we test. Accuracy plotted against scorer depth follows the same curve on every model ( Figure 1 ): shallow scorers fail, the last layer is unreliable, and the best single scorer sits at mid-depth. The mechanism is simple: a layer judges evictions well once it has used the question to find the answer, while shallow layers have not yet done so. Building on this idea, we propose a predictive model with no free parameters that reproduces the measured curves and selects the scoring layer. On models with cross-layer KV sharing, hereafter shared-cache models ( Brandon et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2024 ; Gemma Team, 2025 ; Gemma Team, 2026 ) , one cache serves several reader layers and the scores come by construction from the cache’s writer , its shallowest reader. A shallow writer scores from the region where the curve collapses.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: 1. The depth curve. We measure the depth curve on eighteen per-layer models (0.5B–109B, four labs; two repeated at 32K context; Section 3 ): scoring quality peaks at a middle depth that is stable within a family (0.64–0.75 on Qwen2.5 from 14B up; 0.42–0.59 on Mistral and Llama-3). Shallow scoring is catastrophic ( − 25 -25 to − 56 -56 percentage points, pp), and the own-layer default never significantly beats the best mid-depth scorer. We find the same curve on real documents: on financial-filing extraction, the layer we select on RULER gains 8 and 12pp over the default on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B ( Section 5.2 ). 2. A better SnapKV. We change two things in SnapKV, and each helps on its own in most settings: scoring from a mid-depth layer, and keeping one set of tokens for all heads. Together they beat per-head SnapKV (as implemented in the kvpress library) by + 18 +18 to + 43 +43 pp at budgets of 5 to 15% on five of the seven per-layer models we test (0.5B through 14B) and tie it on the two Llama models ( Section 4.1 ). On financial filings at 32K they beat it on both families, by 14 and 16pp. From 32B up we detect no gain over the default, which is already close to the best mid-depth layer ( Section 5.2 ). 3. A mechanism and a predictive model. Without the question, every layer is nearly equally blind to the answer; with it, attention on the answer builds over depth and peaks at mid-depth. We compute the probability that the answer survives the scorer’s top- k k cut, and it reproduces the measured curves and the reader ranking on the shared-cache model. It also selects the scoring layer: the pick is the best layer measured on fourteen of the eighteen per-layer models and never significantly below it on the other four ( Section 5 ). 4. The shared-cache penalty. On Gemma-4-E2B the shallow writer scores the shared cache by default and needs roughly twice a mid-depth reader’s budget. A sibling design whose writer sits at mid-depth shows no significant penalty, so the writer’s depth is the likely cause. The penalty replicates across budgets, tasks, context lengths, checkpoints, and on Gemma-3n ( Section 6 ).

sections.heading: Attention-scored eviction.
sections.text: These methods score with accumulated attention, recent-window attention, adjusted softmax, or analytic estimates, and differ in how they spend the budget ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Adnan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Oren et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Devoto et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Within this family the scoring layer never differs: each method scores a cache with the layer it belongs to. SqueezeAttention, PyramidKV, CAKE, LAVa, RippleKV, and MOSAIC vary each layer’s budget while keeping own-layer scores ( Wang et al., 2025c ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Kodavanti & Arveti, 2026 ) ; we compare against PyramidKV in Section 4.1 .

sections.heading: Mid-layer token selection.
sections.text: The closest prior work is GemFilter ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , which selects tokens with an early-middle layer’s attention and then re-runs the model on the shortened prompt. Its layer ablation was the first to show a middle-layer peak, in that recompression setting; ASL ( Taniguchi et al., 2026 ) picks the selection layer per input there. Multimodal models prune visual tokens the same way, with a middle layer’s attention, and MAP ( Sun et al., 2026 ) picks that layer per input. FastKV ( Jo et al., 2026 ) forwards only the tokens a mid-depth layer selects to the layers after it, and LazyLLM ( Fu et al., 2024 ) prunes tokens layer by layer during prefill; both speed up prefill and leave each layer scoring its own cache. Eviction is a different setting: no second forward pass, one memory budget for every method, and a default (each layer scoring its own cache) with no counterpart in recompression. The finding that this default loses is new. Section 4.1 reports a head-to-head at the same decode-time memory. HySparse and LongCat Sparse Attention hard-code the choice at training time: each sparse layer takes a preceding layer’s selections ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Zan et al., 2026 ) , which is the writer’s role in Section 6 . At decode time, TidalDecode ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and InfiniGen ( Lee et al., 2024 ) also move selection across layers; neither asks which depth selects best.

sections.heading: Cross-layer KV sharing and compression.
sections.text: CLA, YOCO, LCKV, and the Gemma-3n and Gemma-4 line made one cache serve many layers ( Brandon et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2024 ; Wu & Tu, 2024 ; Gemma Team, 2025 ; Gemma Team, 2026 ) . That is the regime this paper studies. xKV and CommonKV exploit cross-layer redundancy for compression after the fact ( Chang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . None of them decides what an architecturally shared cache should evict.

sections.heading: Per-head differences.
sections.text: RazorAttention, DuoAttention, FastGen, and HeadKV show that, within a layer, different heads need different tokens retained ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Ge et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . DuoAttention calibrates its heads on synthetic prompts with known answer spans, the style our layer selection reuses at layer level ( Section 5 ). A shared cache with multi-query attention removes that freedom: its readers share one physical cache, which can hold only one set of kept tokens. Per-head selections also carry a memory cost of their own: stored as masks they keep the full cache, and heads sharing one buffer keep the union of their picks ( Shi & Gu, 2026 ; Inbasekaran S, 2026 ) . Table 1 shows that a single set scored from the right layer beats per-head selection even where per-head budgets remain possible.

sections.heading: Scoring.
sections.text: The importance of context token j j under scorer layer ℓ \ell is the mean softmax attention that a window of queries places on token j j . The depth curves and the shared-cache results take that window from the question block and average over heads (the question-window convention). The baseline comparison of Section 4.1 instead follows the kvpress implementations, under their own window. The same scorer at the same budget shifts by several points between the two windows, so we never compare numbers across the two windows.

sections.heading: Eviction.
sections.text: A budget b b keeps k = ⌊ b ​ T c ⌋ k=\lfloor b\,T_{c}\rfloor of a prompt’s T c T_{c} context tokens in every layer’s KV cache and masks the rest. Some tokens are always kept, and they count against k k . Under the question window these are the sink (first 4) and the recency window (last 32) ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) ; under kvpress’s window, the scoring window itself. All methods compete at the same k k . Each model is reported at its binding budget , the smallest candidate budget at which the own-layer default loses at least 5pp to the uncompressed model while no task collapses (default recall under 5%): eviction costs accuracy but leaves signal to compare scorers. At these budgets the default has lost 7 to 41pp ( Section A.1 ). The three weakest primary models (15%) and the Gemma-4 shared cache (15% in Figure 1 , 10% in Table 3 ) are shown at uniform budgets; their binding budgets are 15 to 25%, and the gains hold there ( Section A.1 ). We compress after prefill, so the savings apply to the cache that persists through decode. We mask evicted context positions at decode ( − ∞ -\infty additive mask, per-layer and per-head where the baseline requires). Masking preserves RoPE positions and is mathematically equivalent to deleting the rows ( Appendix B ).

sections.heading: Models, tasks, metrics.
sections.text: We study twenty-one models: eighteen with per-layer caches and three with shared caches (Gemma-4-E2B, Gemma-4-E4B, Gemma-3n-E2B). The primary set is six instruction-tuned per-layer models (Qwen2.5-{0.5B,1.5B,7B}, SmolLM2-1.7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B) and Gemma-4-E2B (base checkpoint; the instruct one replicates, Section A.7 ), where the writer plays the “own layer”; twelve more per-layer models extend the range of scale and release date under the same setup ( Table 2 ). The benchmarks are RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) at 4K, 8K, 16K, and 32K, LongBench v1 ( Bai et al., 2024 ) , and DocFinQA ( Reddy et al., 2024 ) , numeric questions over 10-K filings ( Section A.9 ). Every primary RULER result pools the same eight RULER-4096 tasks (five needle-retrieval variants, variable tracking, two QA) and, for each model, counts only the informative ones, those the uncompressed model gets at least 30% right (all eight, on every per-layer model). Adding the other five RULER tasks shrinks every gain and does not change any conclusion ( Section A.3 ). Decoding is greedy. RULER is scored as recall: the fraction of a prompt’s gold answers that appear in the output. The LongBench and DocFinQA metrics are in Sections A.6 and A.9 .

sections.heading: Statistics.
sections.text: Results use 25 prompts per task, n = 200 n{=}200 for the eight-task pool. Prompts are nested in tasks, so all primary confidence intervals are two-stage cluster bootstraps (resample tasks, then prompts). Bold numbers and filled markers mean the paired difference’s 95% interval excludes zero (clustered-significant, for short). Percentile bootstraps can undercover at K = 8 K{=}8 tasks, so the six primary comparisons are also checked with an exact sign-flip test ( Section A.10 ). No multiple-comparison correction is applied. Appendix A records how each budget was set and how each pick performed.

sections.heading: 4 The Depth of the Scoring Layer
sections.text: Figure 1 is the paper’s central result. We let one layer at a time score every cache and plot accuracy against that layer’s depth. On each per-layer model we test seven grid layers, at depths 0.08, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70, 0.85, and 1.0, plus extra layers near the peak, including the survival model’s pick when it is not a grid layer. The curve has the same shape on every model: a cliff on the shallow side, a peak at 0.4–0.75 of depth, and a decline toward the last layer. The default loses to the best mid-depth layer on all seven models, significantly on the four in the top row. The diamonds mark the survival model’s pick ( Section 5 ), chosen from prefill attention and known answer locations on calibration prompts. The picked layer beats the default by + 11.8 +11.8 pp (SmolLM2), + 26.6 +26.6 pp (1.5B), and + 31.4 +31.4 pp (0.5B) on the top row’s three per-layer models, and on the shared-cache panel the best reader recovers + 36.7 +36.7 pp over the writer, all clustered-significant. The three models whose gain is not significant (3B, 7B, 8B) are considered in Section 5.2 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Against the existing methods
sections.text: The depth curves use our question-window scoring. Table 1 re-tests the gains inside SnapKV as kvpress runs it: the last 64 prefilled tokens are the query window ( Appendix B ), scores are smoothed over 5 tokens, and each head keeps its own token set. All methods share one memory budget. The last three methods change SnapKV’s two defaults, one at a time and then together: one kept set for all heads, scoring from the survival model’s pick, and both. On its own, the mid layer helps in every column and the single set in every column but the 14B ( Table A5 ). The combination scores above either alone in every column. It beats per-head SnapKV by + 18 +18 to + 43 +43 pp, clustered-significant in every column (exact tests in Section A.10 ), and recovers 83 to 99% of the uncompressed accuracy where SnapKV keeps 37 to 63%. Beyond these columns the combination wins on Qwen2.5-0.5B and ties on the two Llama models, whose depth gains are not significant either ( Table A4 ). On the 1.5B the lead holds from 5% to 50%: it peaks at 10%, then shrinks as SnapKV recovers, and stays significant throughout ( Section A.4 ). AdaKV, which redistributes budget across heads using SnapKV’s scores, stays within 4.8pp of SnapKV in these columns and differs significantly in one ( Table A5 ). PyramidKV shrinks per-layer budgets with depth, following its authors’ schedule. At the same total memory it scores below SnapKV in every column of Table 1 ( − 8.2 -8.2 to − 29.4 -29.4 pp): PyramidKV’s schedule costs more here than ignoring depth. sections.heading: Recompression head-to-head.
sections.text: GemFilter ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , the nearest competing method, selects tokens with one layer’s attention and re-runs the model on them alone; its layer is fixed at a set fraction of depth (L11 here). With the same decode-time cache size (Qwen2.5-1.5B, 15%), it reaches 36.5 % 36.5\% against our 89.3 % 89.3\% (L20 under the question window, as in Figure 1 ; ceiling 90.8 % 90.8\% ; clustered-significant). The layer explains the gap: GemFilter moved to L20 reaches 91.4 % 91.4\% , within noise of the uncompressed model and of our eviction, which needs no second prefill. GemFilter targets far longer prompts; the comparison holds in our setting only.

sections.heading: 5 The Model: Eviction as Top- k k Selection
sections.text: Figure 2: The survival model predicts the depth curve. Blue: observed accuracy at the measured layers, on and off the seven-layer grid, with task-clustered 95% CIs. Orange dashed: predicted survival S ^ ℓ \hat{S}_{\ell} ( Equation 1 ) from the uncompressed model’s prefill attention, computed at every layer. Diamonds: the survival model’s pick, at its observed accuracy. Last panel: the same construction on the Gemma-4 shared cache, one point per reader. Eviction is a ranking problem: when one layer ℓ \ell scores every cache, the kept set is the top k k of its scores, so ℓ \ell is a good scorer when it ranks the tokens the answer needs above k k -th place. For each prompt we reconstruct the set K ℓ K_{\ell} of tokens layer ℓ \ell would keep, including the always-kept sink and recency tokens. A gold answer survives if some occurrence of it lies entirely inside K ℓ K_{\ell} , matching the metric’s all-or-nothing credit. The prediction is survival averaged over a prompt’s gold answers, then over prompts, S ^ ℓ = 1 n ​ ∑ prompts 1 | G | ​ ∑ g ∈ G { ∃ o ∈ O g : o ⊆ K ℓ } , \hat{S}_{\ell}\;=\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\text{prompts}}\;\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{\exists\,o\in O_{g}:\;o\subseteq K_{\ell}\right\}, (1) where G G is the prompt’s gold set and O g O_{g} the token-index sets of gold g g ’s occurrences. Everything on the right side comes from the prefill attention of the uncompressed model and the locations of the gold spans. It needs no generation and has no adjustable constants; we call it the survival model . It is computed on 25 calibration prompts per task, drawn from dataset rows the evaluation never uses. Figure 2 overlays S ^ ℓ \hat{S}_{\ell} on the depth curves. The survival model’s pick is the layer with the highest S ^ ℓ \hat{S}_{\ell} . When the top two layers differ by less than one standard error of their paired per-prompt difference, S ^ ℓ \hat{S}_{\ell} cannot separate them, and the pick is the shallower of the two: S ^ ℓ \hat{S}_{\ell} counts only the answer span, and a deeper scorer can drop other context the model needs. The pick (diamonds in Figure 2 ) is the best layer measured on fourteen of the eighteen per-layer models and never significantly below it on the other four ( Table A2 ). On the six per-layer models in Figure 2 , S ^ ℓ \hat{S}_{\ell} tracks the measured curves with a Spearman correlation of 0.90 0.90 – 1.00 1.00 and a mean absolute error of 2.7 2.7 – 7.4 7.4 pp. We also compute S ^ ℓ \hat{S}_{\ell} from each reader’s attention over the Gemma-4 shared cache; it reproduces all five readers’ accuracies within 5.1 5.1 pp ( r = 0.998 r{=}0.998 ; Figure 2 , last panel), so the per-layer curves and the shared-cache penalty are one phenomenon.

sections.heading: 5.1 The mechanism
sections.text: Our explanation for the middle peak is that the network needs several layers to find the answer with the question. Early layers have not finished that work, so their attention cannot yet pick out what the question needs. The last layer has moved on to producing output. The layers in between use the question to retrieve, so their attention ranks tokens well. The cliffs at both ends come from the all-or-nothing rule: an answer survives only if every one of its tokens is kept, so moderate ranking errors add up to lost answers. Figure 3: Taking the question away flattens the depth signal. Attention mass on the answer’s tokens, scored by the question block (blue) or the context’s last 32 tokens (orange); means over the 199 prompts with located answer spans, no eviction. Left: Qwen2.5-7B by scorer depth. Right: mass at each model’s peak layer, with and without the question; the number above each pair is their ratio. The direct test is to take the question away. Every depth-curve score in this paper comes from attention paid by the question’s tokens ( Section 3 ). For the test we compute the same attention from the context’s own final tokens instead, as if no question had been asked, and compare how much attention mass each layer places on the answer’s tokens. With the question, Gemma-4’s reader layers place 2.4 × 2.4\times as much mass on the answer as the writer does. Without it, the readers and the writer are nearly equally blind to the answer, and the gap between them shrinks by a factor of 6.5 6.5 . Figure 3 shows the same collapse on the per-layer models. On the two weakest models, Qwen2.5-0.5B and SmolLM2, the drop is small: there the needle draws much of its attention simply by standing out from the surrounding text, with or without the question. With the question, the mass on the answer peaks at mid-depth, within one grid step of the accuracy peak, on every model we test.

sections.heading: Heads versus depth.
sections.text: Retrieval heads concentrate at mid-depth ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , so the depth curve could simply reflect where they sit. As a control, we score every cache with the pooled attention of the sixteen heads with the most attention mass on the answer, chosen on two calibration prompts per task. The head scorer beats the default on all three models tested. It ties the best layer on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.1-8B and beats a mid layer on Mistral-Small-24B, where good and poor layers interleave ( Section A.8 ). The good heads live at mid-depth on every model. A single layer collects them without a head search, and choosing heads within that region would refine the pick.

sections.heading: 5.2 Where the advantage holds and where it ends
sections.text: The three models of Figure 1 ’s bottom row show no significant pooled gain. On the 7B and the 8B the default already ties the mid-depth plateau. On the 3B, gains on the multi-needle tasks offset losses on variable tracking and QA.

sections.heading: Scale.
sections.text: The mid-depth gain persists to 14B and is undetectable from 32B ( Table 2 ). Significant gains of + 12 +12 to + 31 +31 pp below 2B continue at 14B ( + 17.7 +17.7 pp at the pick, L30). The cost of a wrong scorer does not shrink: the worst layer loses 25 to 56pp at every scale. This matters when the architecture fixes the scorer ( Section 6 ) or a deployment adopts one scorer without checking it. sections.heading: Newer families, hybrid attention, and MoE.
sections.text: The curve and the shrinking margin replicate on the 2025–2026 releases ( Table 2 ). On Qwen3 all three sizes peak at a middle depth, and the margin falls with capability: significant at 0.6B, not significant at 1.7B, gone at 14B. The curve also holds on Qwen3.5-9B, where gated linear attention leaves only 8 of 32 layers with a KV cache, and on the mixture-of-experts Llama-4-Scout (109B), whose layers without positional encoding score like their neighbors ( Section A.2 ).

sections.heading: Task family.
sections.text: The curve carries to real documents when exact values must survive the cut. On DocFinQA ( Reddy et al., 2024 ) , the layer selected on RULER at 32K (the RULER pick ) beats the default significantly on both Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, by 8 and 12pp, and each pick lies at its family’s usual depth ( Section A.9 ). Against per-head SnapKV the combination of Table 1 wins there too, by + 13.8 +13.8 and + 15.9 +15.9 pp ( Table A4 ). Open-book question answering keeps the curve’s ends but loses its gain: on LongBench the shallow and last layers still lose, by 5 to 6 F1, and no mid layer beats the default ( Section A.6 ). The survival model, which was built for exact-match answers, does not predict that outcome. The RULER pool splits the same way at 4K and at 32K: the margin over SnapKV comes from the needle tasks and variable tracking; the two QA tasks add little on the small models and lose up to 12pp on the larger ones ( Table A5 ).

sections.heading: Context length.
sections.text: At 32K the curve keeps its shape and its family depth: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B peak at their picks, L14 and L19. The shallow third and the last layer sit 20 to 48pp below the default, and the best layer ties it ( Table 2 ). Table 1 ’s comparison repeats its 4K outcome: the combination beats SnapKV by + 32.5 +32.5 pp on Qwen2.5-7B and ties it on Llama-3.1-8B ( Table A4 ). Eviction binds only at 0.5% and 1%, which keep 160 to 330 tokens, about what the 4K budgets keep ( Table A1 ): pressure depends on the number of kept tokens rather than their fraction of the context.

On E2B the writer is layer 14 of 35 (depth 0.41), the shallowest of the five readers, and it sits on the shallow side of the curve ( Figure 1 ); the deeper readers place 2.4 × 2.4\times as much question-driven mass on the answer as it does ( Section 5.1 ). sections.heading: The penalty follows the writer’s depth.
sections.text: Gemma-4-E4B, a sibling design, places its writer at depth 0.56. On E4B the penalty largely disappears: the + 22.2 +22.2 pp consensus-over-writer gain of Table 3 shrinks to + 6.3 +6.3 pp [ − 3.2 , + 17.1 ] [-3.2,+17.1] at the same 10% budget, and the task-paired difference between the two designs is + 15.9 +15.9 pp [ + 4.5 , + 28.2 ] [+4.5,+28.2] . Beyond retrieval the evidence weakens. On LongBench (seven datasets) consensus beats the writer on E2B-it by + 8.4 +8.4 F1 [ + 1.6 , + 17.1 ] [+1.6,+17.1] , but the two designs do not differ significantly there. On DocFinQA, E4B-it’s mid-depth writer beats every deeper reader by 14 to 22pp ( Section A.9 ): when the writer already sits at mid-depth, the architecture has picked well.

sections.heading: 7 Practical Guidance, Cost, and Limitations
sections.text: On per-layer models, let the survival model choose the scoring layer ( Section 5 ) and let that layer score every cache with a single set of kept tokens. Do not average across all layers: rank consensus over all layers loses 21–37pp to the selected layer on two models ( Section A.5 ). On shared-cache models with a shallow writer, score with a mid-depth reader or with rank consensus over the cache’s readers. Scoring reads one layer’s attention at prefill and adds under 1% to its time ( Appendix B ). Physical eviction at a 1% budget shrinks Llama-3.1-8B’s 32K decode-resident cache from 4.0GB to 45MB and speeds decode 1.4 × 1.4\times ( Appendix B ). The evidence has limits. The pick needs calibration prompts with known answers. The shared-cache results come only from Gemma models, the scale trend on newer releases only from Qwen3, and the 70B and 72B runs from 4-bit NF4 checkpoints. Three problems remain open. First, the best scorer differs by task family ( Section 5.2 ), so a selector that detects the task family at prefill could beat any single layer. Second, the writer-depth explanation rests on one sibling pair ( Section 6 ). Training the same model with a deeper writer would test it directly. Third, every scorer here sees the question, and SnapKV’s edge disappears without it ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , so prefix caches need a question-free signal ( Kim et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: RULER prompts at 4K–16K come from the simonjegou/ruler Hugging Face release and at 32K from lighteval’s official-generator releases, one per tokenizer (e.g. lighteval/RULER-32768-Lamma3-Instruct ). Models run in fp16, except Llama-4-Scout and Qwen3.5-9B in bf16 and the 70B and 72B in 4-bit NF4. Prompt draws are deterministic. Greedy decoding is bit-exact only within one GPU and kernel configuration: rerunning the primary sweeps on a different GPU flipped a few near-tied prompts per configuration and moved pooled accuracies by at most a point. Every number is computed by a script and stored in a JSON file; figures, tables, and the statistics quoted as macros read these files, and the prose numbers come from those tables and files. One statistics implementation is shared by every figure and table. Baseline semantics were ported from the kvpress reference implementations ( https://github.com/NVIDIA/kvpress , version 0.5.4; PyramidKV’s schedule from its authors’ code), and Appendix B verifies that masked eviction matches physical deletion. On the same prompts, our SnapKV scoring and kvpress agree on over 99.8% of kept tokens (Llama-3.1-8B).

sections.heading: A.9 Financial-filing extraction
sections.text: DocFinQA ( Reddy et al., 2024 ) asks numeric questions about full 10-K filings. Each question comes with the arithmetic steps that produce its answer; the gold set is the figures those steps take from the filing, as they appear there. The model sees a 31.5K-token slice that contains them at a random offset and is asked to state the figures it uses; we score recall of those figures. The uncompressed model scores under 50% on this task, so the binding budget’s 5% collapse threshold is too low to be useful. The budget here is the smallest scanned one at which the default keeps at least 30% of its uncompressed recall. With one task there is nothing to cluster, so the intervals are prompt-level bootstraps. Table A9 gives the depth curves. The layer picked on RULER transfers: it beats the default significantly on both per-layer models, and the curve peaks in the same region as on RULER while the other family’s depth loses, so the good depth belongs to the model family rather than the task. Picking the layer on the task itself gains little: the on-task pick, the layer where attention mass on the answer peaks, ties the RULER pick on Qwen2.5-7B and sits one layer beside it on Llama-3.1-8B (L13 against L14; chosen on 25 prompts and tested on the other 175, where it beats the default by + 12.3 +12.3 pp). On Gemma-4-E4B-it the mid-depth writer is already the best scorer and every deeper reader loses, consistent with Section 6 , where the penalty follows the writer’s depth; a shared cache has no scorer shallower than its writer, so only the deep half of the curve is covered. sections.heading: Appendix B Eviction, scoring window, and cost
sections.text: The main-text experiments mask evicted rows rather than deleting them, which lets the kept set vary per layer and per head. Masking is exact: softmax with − ∞ -\infty entries equals softmax over the kept subset. We checked it by rerunning the single set scored from L19 on Qwen2.5-1.5B (15% budget, the eight-task pool, n = 200 n{=}200 ) with the evicted rows physically removed: accuracy is identical on all 200 prompts, and 171 generations are token-identical. The other 29 differ from some token on, as fp16 arithmetic over different tensor shapes allows when two candidates are nearly tied, and none changes the answer.

sections.heading: Scoring convention.
sections.text: Every scorer uses attention from a prefill of the prompt without its final token. The cache is then compressed, and that final token is decoded under the mask like every generated token. The kvpress window of Section 4.1 is therefore the 64 prompt tokens preceding the final one. GemFilter’s statistic is defined on the final token itself, so Section 4.1 takes its scores from a full-prompt prefill.

sections.heading: Runtime and memory.
sections.text: The Section 7 cost numbers come from Llama-3.1-8B in fp16 on one H200, five prompts per context length, the first as warm-up and medians over the other four. Scoring as deployed captures one layer’s queries and keys during the ordinary prefill, which matches a plain prefill within timing noise at both lengths. The saving arrives at decode: at 32K and a 1% budget the decode-resident cache falls from 3.96GB to 45MB and decoding runs 1.40 × 1.40\times faster (81 to 113 tokens/s); at 4K and 5%, from 0.45GB to 27MB for 1.08 × 1.08\times . Peak prefill memory is unchanged, because eviction happens after prefill. On Qwen2.5-1.5B at 4K, scoring from one layer costs 0.16ms and the top- k k selection 0.06ms, together under 1% of a prefill that takes 31 to 54ms across prompts; scoring all 28 layers, as the own-layer default does, costs 4.3ms.

Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction Ekaterina Seregina Affiliation: Colby College Email: eseregin@colby.edu Abstract Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top- k k cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default. 1 Introduction The KV cache is the memory cost of long-context inference, and eviction is the simplest way to shrink it: score every cached token, keep the top k k , drop the rest. Existing methods differ in how they score and how they spend the budget ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Cai et al., 2024 ) , but all take scores from the layer whose cache is pruned: layer 7 judges what layer 7 keeps. The scoring layer is a hyperparameter that, to our knowledge, no eviction method varies or reports. We find that the chosen layer’s depth governs eviction quality at every scale we test. Accuracy plotted against scorer depth follows the same curve on every model ( Figure 1 ): shallow scorers fail, the last layer is unreliable, and the best single scorer sits at mid-depth. The mechanism is simple: a layer judges evictions well once it has used the question to find the answer, while shallow layers have not yet done so. Building on this idea, we propose a predictive model with no free parameters that reproduces the measured curves and selects the scoring layer. A better SnapKV. We change two things in SnapKV, and each helps on its own in most settings: scoring from a mid-depth layer, and keeping one set of tokens for all heads. A mechanism and a predictive model. Without the question, every layer is nearly equally blind to the answer; with it, attention on the answer builds over depth and peaks at mid-depth. We compute the probability that the answer survives the scorer’s top- k k cut, and it reproduces the measured curves and the reader ranking on the shared-cache model. It also selects the scoring layer: the pick is the best layer measured on fourteen of the eighteen per-layer models and never significantly below it on the other four ( Section 5 ). 4. The penalty replicates across budgets, tasks, context lengths, checkpoints, and on Gemma-3n ( Section 6 ). 2 Related Work Attention-scored eviction. These methods score with accumulated attention, recent-window attention, adjusted softmax, or analytic estimates, and differ in how they spend the budget ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Adnan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Oren et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Devoto et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Within this family the scoring layer never differs: each method scores a cache with the layer it belongs to. SqueezeAttention, PyramidKV, CAKE, LAVa, RippleKV, and MOSAIC vary each layer’s budget while keeping own-layer scores ( Wang et al., 2025c ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Kodavanti & Arveti, 2026 ) ; we compare against PyramidKV in Section 4.1 . Mid-layer token selection. The closest prior work is GemFilter ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , which selects tokens with an early-middle layer’s attention and then re-runs the model on the shortened prompt. Its layer ablation was the first to show a middle-layer peak, in that recompression setting; ASL ( Taniguchi et al., 2026 ) picks the selection layer per input there. Multimodal models prune visual tokens the same way, with a middle layer’s attention, and MAP ( Sun et al., 2026 ) picks that layer per input. FastKV ( Jo et al., 2026 ) forwards only the tokens a mid-depth layer selects to the layers after it, and LazyLLM ( Fu et al., 2024 ) prunes tokens layer by layer during prefill; both speed up prefill and leave each layer scoring its own cache. Eviction is a different setting: no second forward pass, one memory budget for every method, and a default (each layer scoring its own cache) with no counterpart in recompression. The finding that this default loses is new. Section 4.1 reports a head-to-head at the same decode-time memory. HySparse and LongCat Sparse Attention hard-code the choice at training time: each sparse layer takes a preceding layer’s selections ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Zan et al., 2026 ) , which is the writer’s role in Section 6 . At decode time, TidalDecode ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and InfiniGen ( Lee et al., 2024 ) also move selection across layers; neither asks which depth selects best. Cross-layer KV sharing and compression. CLA, YOCO, LCKV, and the Gemma-3n and Gemma-4 line made one cache serve many layers ( Brandon et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2024 ; Wu & Tu, 2024 ; Gemma Team, 2025 ; Gemma Team, 2026 ) . That is the regime this paper studies. xKV and CommonKV exploit cross-layer redundancy for compression after the fact ( Chang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . None of them decides what an architecturally shared cache should evict. Per-head differences. RazorAttention, DuoAttention, FastGen, and HeadKV show that, within a layer, different heads need different tokens retained ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Ge et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . DuoAttention calibrates its heads on synthetic prompts with known answer spans, the style our layer selection reuses at layer level ( Section 5 ). A shared cache with multi-query attention removes that freedom: its readers share one physical cache, which can hold only one set of kept tokens. Per-head selections also carry a memory cost of their own: stored as masks they keep the full cache, and heads sharing one buffer keep the union of their picks ( Shi & Gu, 2026 ; Inbasekaran S, 2026 ) . Early layers have not finished that work, so their attention cannot yet pick out what the question needs. The last layer has moved on to producing output. The layers in between use the question to retrieve, so their attention ranks tokens well. The cliffs at both ends come from the all-or-nothing rule: an answer survives only if every one of its tokens is kept, so moderate ranking errors add up to lost answers. On DocFinQA, E4B-it’s mid-depth writer beats every deeper reader by 14 to 22pp ( Section A.9 ): when the writer already sits at mid-depth, the architecture has picked well. 7 Practical Guidance, Cost, and Limitations On per-layer models, let the survival model choose the scoring layer ( Section 5 ) and let that layer score every cache with a single set of kept tokens. Do not average across all layers: rank consensus over all layers loses 21–37pp to the selected layer on two models ( Section A.5 ). On shared-cache models with a shallow writer, score with a mid-depth reader or with rank consensus over the cache’s readers. Scoring reads one layer’s attention at prefill and adds under 1% to its time ( Appendix B ). Physical eviction at a 1% budget shrinks Llama-3.1-8B’s 32K decode-resident cache from 4.0GB to 45MB and speeds decode 1.4 × 1.4\times ( Appendix B ). The evidence has limits. The pick needs calibration prompts with known answers. The shared-cache results come only from Gemma models, the scale trend on newer releases only from Qwen3, and the 70B and 72B runs from 4-bit NF4 checkpoints. Three problems remain open. First, the best scorer differs by task family ( Section 5.2 ), so a selector that detects the task family at prefill could beat any single layer. Second, the writer-depth explanation rests on one sibling pair ( Section 6 ). Training the same model with a deeper writer would test it directly. Third, every scorer here sees the question, and SnapKV’s edge disappears without it ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , so prefix caches need a question-free signal ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Appendix B Eviction, scoring window, and cost The main-text experiments mask evicted rows rather than deleting them, which lets the kept set vary per layer and per head. Masking is exact: softmax with − ∞ -\infty entries equals softmax over the kept subset. We checked it by rerunning the single set scored from L19 on Qwen2.5-1.5B (15% budget, the eight-task pool, n = 200 n{=}200 ) with the evicted rows physically removed: accuracy is identical on all 200 prompts, and 171 generations are token-identical. The other 29 differ from some token on, as fp16 arithmetic over different tensor shapes allows when two candidates are nearly tied, and none changes the answer. Scoring convention. Every scorer uses attention from a prefill of the prompt without its final token. The cache is then compressed, and that final token is decoded under the mask like every generated token. The kvpress window of Section 4.1 is therefore the 64 prompt tokens preceding the final one. GemFilter’s statistic is defined on the final token itself, so Section 4.1 takes its scores from a full-prompt prefill. Runtime and memory. The Section 7 cost numbers come from Llama-3.1-8B in fp16 on one H200, five prompts per context length, the first as warm-up and medians over the other four. Scoring as deployed captures one layer’s queries and keys during the ordinary prefill, which matches a plain prefill within timing noise at both lengths. The saving arrives at decode: at 32K and a 1% budget the decode-resident cache falls from 3.96GB to 45MB and decoding runs 1.40 × 1.40\times faster (81 to 113 tokens/s); at 4K and 5%, from 0.45GB to 27MB for 1.08 × 1.08\times . Peak prefill memory is unchanged, because eviction happens after prefill. On Qwen2.5-1.5B at 4K, scoring from one layer costs 0.16ms and the top- k k selection 0.06ms, together under 1% of a prefill that takes 31 to 54ms across prompts; scoring all 28 layers, as the own-layer default does, costs 4.3ms.
